title: Experimental Physical/Inorganic Chemistry
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned 200L laboratory curriculum pairing physical-chemistry measurement techniques (viscosity, surface tension, conductometry, potentiometry/pH-metry, adsorption) with systematic qualitative inorganic analysis (cation/anion group tests, flame tests, confirmatory tests, and simple inorganic complex preparation).

questions.question: In the Ostwald viscometer method, the relative viscosity of a liquid compared with water is determined mainly by measuring:
options: The mass of each liquid at a fixed volume only
The time taken for a fixed volume of each liquid to flow between two calibration marks under its own weight, at the same temperature
The colour intensity of each liquid
The boiling point of each liquid
questions.correct_answer: The time taken for a fixed volume of each liquid to flow between two calibration marks under its own weight, at the same temperature
questions.explanation: In Poiseuille-based viscometry, viscosity is proportional to the flow time and density of the liquid for a fixed viscometer geometry, so relative viscosity is obtained by comparing flow times (and densities) of the test liquid and a reference liquid such as water.

questions.question: Why must the Ostwald viscometer and the liquids being compared be kept at a constant, controlled temperature (e.g. in a thermostatted water bath) during the experiment?
options: Viscosity is essentially independent of temperature so this step is unnecessary
Viscosity is strongly temperature-dependent (generally decreasing as temperature rises), so uncontrolled temperature variation would introduce significant error
It only affects the colour of the liquid
It is required solely to dissolve the sample
questions.correct_answer: Viscosity is strongly temperature-dependent (generally decreasing as temperature rises), so uncontrolled temperature variation would introduce significant error
questions.explanation: Liquid viscosity decreases markedly with increasing temperature as intermolecular forces are more easily overcome, so precise, reproducible viscosity measurements require a constant-temperature bath.

questions.question: A stalagmometer is used in the laboratory to measure a liquid's:
options: Viscosity directly
Surface tension, by counting the number of drops formed from a fixed volume of liquid
Refractive index
Electrical conductivity
questions.correct_answer: Surface tension, by counting the number of drops formed from a fixed volume of liquid
questions.explanation: A stalagmometer measures surface tension by comparing the number of drops (or drop weight) formed by a fixed volume of the test liquid with that of a reference liquid of known surface tension, since drop size depends on surface tension.

questions.question: Adding a small amount of soap or detergent (a surfactant) to water generally causes its surface tension to:
options: Increase sharply
Decrease, because surfactant molecules accumulate at the surface and reduce intermolecular attraction there
Remain completely unchanged
Become impossible to measure
questions.correct_answer: Decrease, because surfactant molecules accumulate at the surface and reduce intermolecular attraction there
questions.explanation: Surfactants are amphiphilic and preferentially orient at the air-water interface, disrupting the cohesive hydrogen-bonding network of water molecules at the surface and lowering the surface tension.

questions.question: In a conductometric titration of a strong acid with a strong base, the conductance of the solution initially falls as the base is added, mainly because:
options: The highly mobile H+ ions are progressively replaced by the much less mobile cation of the base's salt
Water is being removed from the solution
The temperature of the solution decreases rapidly
No ions are present in the solution at any stage
questions.correct_answer: The highly mobile H+ ions are progressively replaced by the much less mobile cation of the base's salt
questions.explanation: H+ (and OH-) ions have unusually high ionic mobility due to the Grotthuss mechanism; as they are consumed and replaced by ordinary, less mobile cations/anions, the overall conductance decreases until the equivalence point.

questions.question: In the conductometric titration described above, after the equivalence point the conductance of the solution starts to:
options: Continue decreasing indefinitely
Rise again sharply, as excess highly mobile OH- ions from the added base accumulate in solution
Immediately drop to zero
Remain perfectly constant
questions.correct_answer: Rise again sharply, as excess highly mobile OH- ions from the added base accumulate in solution
questions.explanation: Beyond the equivalence point, further base adds excess OH- ions (also highly mobile) without any further neutralization, so the conductance rises again, giving the characteristic V-shaped conductometric titration curve.

questions.question: The 'cell constant' of a conductivity cell, used to convert a measured conductance into specific conductance (conductivity), is defined as:
options: The ratio of the distance between the electrodes to their cross-sectional area
The resistance of pure water in the cell
The molar mass of the electrolyte used to calibrate it
The applied voltage during measurement
questions.correct_answer: The ratio of the distance between the electrodes to their cross-sectional area
questions.explanation: The cell constant (l/A) relates the measured conductance of a solution to its intrinsic specific conductance (kappa), and is determined by calibrating the cell with a standard KCl solution of known conductivity.

questions.question: A glass electrode used in pH measurement must be calibrated against standard buffer solutions of known pH before use, mainly because:
options: The electrode's response (slope and offset) can drift and vary between electrodes, so calibration corrects the meter reading to a true pH scale
Buffers are needed to clean the electrode surface only
Glass electrodes cannot measure pH without added buffer in the test sample itself
Calibration changes the chemical composition of the sample being tested
questions.correct_answer: The electrode's response (slope and offset) can drift and vary between electrodes, so calibration corrects the meter reading to a true pH scale
questions.explanation: The glass electrode generates a potential related to pH via the Nernst equation, but its exact slope and offset vary with age and condition, so calibration against standard buffers of known pH ensures accurate readings.

questions.question: In a potentiometric (pH-metric) titration of a weak acid with a strong base, the pKa of the weak acid can be estimated directly from the titration curve as the pH at:
options: The very start of the titration, before any base is added
The half-equivalence point, where half of the acid has been neutralized
The point of maximum conductance
A pH of exactly 7.00 in all cases
questions.correct_answer: The half-equivalence point, where half of the acid has been neutralized
questions.explanation: At the half-equivalence point, the concentrations of the weak acid and its conjugate base are equal, so by the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation, pH = pKa at this point on the titration curve.

questions.question: Compared with an indicator-based acid-base titration, a potentiometric (pH-metric) titration has the practical advantage that it:
options: Can be used with coloured or turbid solutions where a visual indicator colour change would be hard to see
Never requires any calibration
Cannot give the equivalence point at all
Requires no electrical equipment
questions.correct_answer: Can be used with coloured or turbid solutions where a visual indicator colour change would be hard to see
questions.explanation: Because the endpoint is located from the inflection of a measured pH curve rather than a visual colour change, potentiometric titration works well even for deeply coloured or turbid solutions where indicators are unreliable.

questions.question: In the adsorption of acetic acid from solution onto activated charcoal, the extent of adsorption at constant temperature is commonly described by the empirical Freundlich isotherm:
options: x/m = k C^(1/n), relating the mass adsorbed per gram of adsorbent (x/m) to the equilibrium solution concentration (C)
x/m = kT, relating adsorption only to temperature
x/m is always independent of the equilibrium concentration
x/m = k/V, relating adsorption only to the volume of solution used
questions.correct_answer: x/m = k C^(1/n), relating the mass adsorbed per gram of adsorbent (x/m) to the equilibrium solution concentration (C)
questions.explanation: The Freundlich adsorption isotherm is an empirical power-law relationship between the amount adsorbed per unit mass of adsorbent and the equilibrium concentration of adsorbate remaining in solution, with k and n as empirical constants.

questions.question: In the acetic acid/activated-charcoal adsorption experiment, the equilibrium concentration of acetic acid remaining in solution after adsorption is typically determined by:
options: Titrating a filtered portion of the solution against standard sodium hydroxide
Measuring the colour intensity of the solution
Weighing the charcoal before and after only
Measuring the boiling point of the filtrate
questions.correct_answer: Titrating a filtered portion of the solution against standard sodium hydroxide
questions.explanation: After the charcoal has adsorbed some acetic acid and equilibrium is reached, the mixture is filtered and the remaining acid concentration in the filtrate is found by acid-base titration with standard NaOH.

questions.question: In systematic qualitative cation analysis, dilute hydrochloric acid is added first to the sample solution to precipitate 'Group I' cations. Which of the following cations belongs to this group, precipitating as an insoluble chloride?
options: Pb2+ (forming insoluble PbCl2)
Na+
Ca2+
Al3+
questions.correct_answer: Pb2+ (forming insoluble PbCl2)
questions.explanation: Group I cations (Ag+, Hg2^2+, Pb2+) form insoluble chlorides with dilute HCl and are precipitated out first in the classical qualitative analysis scheme, before any other group reagent is applied.

questions.question: In the classical qualitative analysis scheme, 'Group II' cations (e.g. Cu2+, Pb2+ remainder, Cd2+) are precipitated as insoluble sulphides by passing H2S gas into the solution under conditions of:
options: Dilute mineral acid (acidic medium)
Strong ammonia solution (basic medium) only
Pure distilled water with no acid or base
Concentrated sodium hydroxide only
questions.correct_answer: Dilute mineral acid (acidic medium)
questions.explanation: Group II sulphides are much less soluble than Group III-IV sulphides, so they precipitate even in the presence of dilute acid, which suppresses precipitation of the more soluble sulphides of later groups.

questions.question: Ammonium chloride is added along with ammonium hydroxide before precipitating 'Group III' cations (e.g. Fe3+, Al3+, Cr3+) as hydroxides, mainly to:
options: Suppress the ionization/concentration of OH- (via the common-ion effect) so that only Group III hydroxides, and not Group IV/V hydroxides such as Mg(OH)2, are precipitated
Increase the solubility of Group III hydroxides so nothing precipitates
Change the colour of the precipitate
Act only as a drying agent for the final precipitate
questions.correct_answer: Suppress the ionization/concentration of OH- (via the common-ion effect) so that only Group III hydroxides, and not Group IV/V hydroxides such as Mg(OH)2, are precipitated
questions.explanation: NH4Cl provides a common NH4+ ion that suppresses further ionization of NH4OH, keeping the OH- concentration low enough to precipitate only the very insoluble Group III hydroxides while more soluble hydroxides like Mg(OH)2 remain in solution.

questions.question: In qualitative analysis, addition of potassium iodide (KI) solution to a solution containing Pb2+ ions gives a characteristic:
options: Deep blue solution
Bright yellow precipitate of lead(II) iodide (PbI2)
White precipitate that dissolves in excess KI
Colourless solution with no precipitate
questions.correct_answer: Bright yellow precipitate of lead(II) iodide (PbI2)
questions.explanation: Pb2+ reacts with iodide ions to form a bright yellow, sparingly soluble precipitate of lead(II) iodide, a classic confirmatory test for lead ions ('golden rain' when redissolved hot and recrystallized).

questions.question: Addition of excess ammonium hydroxide to a solution of Cu2+ ions produces a characteristic:
options: Deep blue solution due to formation of the tetraamminecopper(II) complex ion, [Cu(NH3)4]2+
White precipitate insoluble in excess ammonia
Brick-red precipitate
Colourless, odourless gas
questions.correct_answer: Deep blue solution due to formation of the tetraamminecopper(II) complex ion, [Cu(NH3)4]2+
questions.explanation: Cu2+ first forms a pale blue Cu(OH)2 precipitate with a little ammonia, which then dissolves in excess ammonia to give the characteristic deep (royal) blue tetraamminecopper(II) complex ion.

questions.question: Addition of potassium thiocyanate (KSCN) solution to a solution suspected of containing Fe3+ ions produces a characteristic:
options: Blood-red colouration due to formation of the [Fe(SCN)]2+ complex
Pale green precipitate
No colour change at all
Yellow precipitate insoluble in acid
questions.correct_answer: Blood-red colouration due to formation of the [Fe(SCN)]2+ complex
questions.explanation: Fe3+ ions form an intensely coloured blood-red thiocyanatoiron(III) complex with SCN-, one of the most sensitive and characteristic confirmatory tests for ferric ions.

questions.question: Addition of aqueous ammonia (NH4OH) to a solution of Al3+ ions gives:
options: A white, gelatinous precipitate of Al(OH)3 that is insoluble in excess ammonia
A deep blue solution
A yellow precipitate
No visible reaction
questions.correct_answer: A white, gelatinous precipitate of Al(OH)3 that is insoluble in excess ammonia
questions.explanation: Al3+ forms a white, gelatinous aluminium hydroxide precipitate with ammonia; unlike some other hydroxides, it does not redissolve in excess ammonia, which helps distinguish Al3+ from cations like Zn2+ or Cu2+ that form soluble ammine complexes.

questions.question: In a flame test for qualitative cation identification, a persistent brick-red flame colouration is characteristic of the presence of:
options: Calcium ions
Sodium ions
Potassium ions
Barium ions
questions.correct_answer: Calcium ions
questions.explanation: Calcium salts impart a characteristic brick-red colour to a non-luminous Bunsen flame, resulting from the specific electronic transitions of thermally excited calcium atoms.

questions.question: In a flame test, a persistent apple-green (or yellowish-green) flame colouration is characteristic of the presence of:
options: Barium ions
Sodium ions
Lithium ions
Copper(II) ions giving a blue-green flame instead
questions.correct_answer: Barium ions
questions.explanation: Barium salts give a characteristic yellowish-green (apple-green) flame colour, one of the standard confirmatory flame tests used in qualitative inorganic analysis.

questions.question: An intense persistent yellow flame colour that can mask other, fainter flame colours (and requires viewing through blue cobalt glass to filter it out) is characteristic of:
options: Sodium ions
Potassium ions
Calcium ions
Strontium ions
questions.correct_answer: Sodium ions
questions.explanation: Even trace amounts of sodium give an intense, persistent yellow flame that can swamp weaker flame colours from other cations, so blue cobalt glass is used to filter out the sodium yellow and reveal, for example, potassium's lilac colour.

questions.question: Addition of dilute hydrochloric acid followed by barium chloride solution to a solution suspected of containing sulphate (SO4^2-) ions produces:
options: A dense white precipitate of barium sulphate that remains insoluble even in excess dilute acid
A yellow precipitate
Effervescence of a colourless gas
No reaction at all
questions.correct_answer: A dense white precipitate of barium sulphate that remains insoluble even in excess dilute acid
questions.explanation: Sulphate ions give a characteristic dense white precipitate of BaSO4 with barium chloride, which (unlike sulphite or carbonate precipitates) does not dissolve in dilute hydrochloric acid, distinguishing sulphate from these other anions.

questions.question: Addition of dilute acid to a solid or solution suspected of containing carbonate (CO3^2-) ions produces brisk effervescence of a gas that:
options: Turns limewater milky (forms a white precipitate of CaCO3), confirming carbon dioxide
Relights a glowing splint
Has a strong pungent, choking smell characteristic of ammonia
Burns with a pop sound when ignited
questions.correct_answer: Turns limewater milky (forms a white precipitate of CaCO3), confirming carbon dioxide
questions.explanation: Carbonates react with dilute acids to liberate CO2 gas, which is confirmed by passing it through limewater (calcium hydroxide solution), turning it milky due to formation of insoluble CaCO3.

questions.question: Addition of silver nitrate (AgNO3) solution to a solution containing chloride (Cl-) ions produces a white precipitate that:
options: Is insoluble in dilute nitric acid but readily dissolves in excess dilute/concentrated ammonia solution
Is bright yellow in colour
Dissolves readily in dilute nitric acid
Turns black immediately in the dark
questions.correct_answer: Is insoluble in dilute nitric acid but readily dissolves in excess dilute/concentrated ammonia solution
questions.explanation: AgCl is a white precipitate insoluble in dilute HNO3 (ruling out carbonate/sulphite interference) but soluble in excess ammonia due to formation of the diamminesilver(I) complex, a standard confirmatory test for chloride.

questions.question: The brown-ring test is a classical confirmatory test for the presence of:
options: Nitrate (NO3-) ions, using freshly prepared iron(II) sulphate solution and concentrated sulphuric acid added carefully down the side of the tube
Sulphate ions only
Chloride ions only
Phosphate ions only
questions.correct_answer: Nitrate (NO3-) ions, using freshly prepared iron(II) sulphate solution and concentrated sulphuric acid added carefully down the side of the tube
questions.explanation: In the brown-ring test, NO3- is reduced by Fe2+ in the presence of concentrated H2SO4 to nitric oxide, which forms a brown ring of the [Fe(NO)]2+ complex at the interface between the two liquid layers, confirming nitrate.

questions.question: Addition of ammonium molybdate solution and dilute nitric acid to a solution containing phosphate (PO4^3-) ions, followed by gentle warming, produces:
options: A canary-yellow precipitate of ammonium phosphomolybdate
A blood-red colouration
Effervescence of a colourless gas
A deep blue precipitate
questions.correct_answer: A canary-yellow precipitate of ammonium phosphomolybdate
questions.explanation: Phosphate ions react with ammonium molybdate in acidic, warm conditions to form a characteristic canary-yellow crystalline precipitate of ammonium phosphomolybdate, a classical confirmatory test for phosphate.

questions.question: In the preparation of a simple inorganic double salt such as ferrous ammonium sulphate (Mohr's salt), the compound is typically crystallized from a solution containing stoichiometric amounts of iron(II) sulphate and ammonium sulphate because the double salt:
options: Is more stable to air oxidation and easier to obtain in pure crystalline form than iron(II) sulphate alone
Cannot be formed from a mixed solution at all
Must be prepared entirely without water
Only forms above 200 degC
questions.correct_answer: Is more stable to air oxidation and easier to obtain in pure crystalline form than iron(II) sulphate alone
questions.explanation: Mohr's salt, FeSO4.(NH4)2SO4.6H2O, is considerably more resistant to aerial oxidation of Fe2+ than simple iron(II) sulphate, making it a more stable, easily purified primary standard for iron(II) in volumetric analysis.

questions.question: In redox confirmatory testing of Fe2+ ions, addition of potassium permanganate solution (acidified with dilute sulphuric acid) to a solution containing Fe2+ results in:
options: Decolourization of the purple permanganate as Fe2+ is oxidised to Fe3+ and Mn7+ is reduced to Mn2+
No visible reaction of any kind
Formation of a permanent purple colour throughout
Immediate formation of a black precipitate
questions.correct_answer: Decolourization of the purple permanganate as Fe2+ is oxidised to Fe3+ and Mn7+ is reduced to Mn2+
questions.explanation: Acidified permanganate oxidises Fe2+ to Fe3+ while itself being reduced from intensely purple MnO4- to nearly colourless Mn2+, so the purple colour disappears as it reacts, until an excess gives a persistent pink tinge at the end point.

questions.question: The borax bead test used in qualitative inorganic analysis identifies certain metal ions by:
options: The characteristic colour of the glassy bead formed when a metal salt is fused with borax in a Bunsen flame, in oxidising and reducing flame conditions
Measuring the melting point of the metal salt directly
Dissolving the salt in water and measuring its pH
Weighing the bead before and after heating
questions.correct_answer: The characteristic colour of the glassy bead formed when a metal salt is fused with borax in a Bunsen flame, in oxidising and reducing flame conditions
questions.explanation: Borax fuses to a clear glassy bead that dissolves small amounts of metal salts, giving characteristic colours (e.g. blue for cobalt, green for chromium/copper in the oxidising flame) that help identify the metal ion present.

questions.question: In the systematic scheme of qualitative inorganic analysis, a 'group reagent' is added at each stage primarily to:
options: Precipitate a specific group of cations together under defined conditions, separating them from cations belonging to later groups
Dissolve all cations present simultaneously
Change the colour of the solution for aesthetic purposes
Neutralize the entire solution to exactly pH 7
questions.correct_answer: Precipitate a specific group of cations together under defined conditions, separating them from cations belonging to later groups
questions.explanation: Each group reagent (e.g. dilute HCl, H2S in acid, NH4OH/NH4Cl) is chosen and applied under specific conditions so that only the cations of that particular group precipitate, allowing systematic, sequential separation and identification.
